steps.tx: Replace **cortisol** before **thyroxine** when hypopituitarism is possible. Thyroid hormone speeds cortisol clearance, so levothyroxine started while cortisol is low can precipitate an adrenal crisis. Give hydrocortisone first if the patient is unwell, and add levothyroxine only after glucocorticoid cover is in place. A low free T4 with a low or normal TSH is central hypothyroidism, and it is not the first drug to start.

steps.tx: In slowly progressive hypopituitarism, **growth hormone** and the **gonadotropins** usually fail before TSH and ACTH. The drawing shows that usual order, with growth hormone first and ACTH later. Apoplexy and hypophysitis break that order, and ACTH deficiency can be the first and most dangerous deficit. Prolactin is often the last to fall, so a woman who still lactates can already lack cortisol.

steps.tx: **Sheehan syndrome** follows severe postpartum haemorrhage with pituitary ischaemia. Failure to lactate and persistent amenorrhea are the classic clues, and other anterior pituitary deficits can appear later. The drawing names failure of postpartum lactation under the prolactin axis. Do not wait for every axis to fail before you replace cortisol, because ACTH deficiency can declare itself during a later illness.

rows: Not proof of hormone loss by itself

steps.tx: **Pituitary apoplexy** is sudden haemorrhage or infarction, often into an existing adenoma. The presentation is a sudden severe headache, visual loss, and acute cortisol deficiency. Give intravenous hydrocortisone as soon as the diagnosis is suspected. Surgery is for deteriorating vision or a falling level of consciousness, and it is not required for every bleed. The film is an enlarged sella with mixed signal and no labels.

steps.tx: **Lymphocytic hypophysitis** often presents in late pregnancy or after delivery. ACTH deficiency is common, the stalk may be thickened, and the gland can imitate a pituitary mass. Hormone replacement is required even when the mass is observed rather than removed. Do not mistake it for Sheehan syndrome: there may be no haemorrhage, and the MRI clue is stalk thickening rather than an empty sella.

right.title: Sheehan syndrome
points: Failure to lactate is the clue

steps.tx: **Immune checkpoint** inhibitor hypophysitis is linked more strongly to **CTLA-4 blockade** than to PD-1 blockade. ACTH deficiency is often permanent. High-dose glucocorticoid treats headache and mass effect, but it does not reliably restore pituitary function. Continue hormone replacement when the cancer drug is working. A tired patient on ipilimumab needs a morning cortisol before the fatigue is blamed on the cancer alone.

steps.tx: Adult **growth hormone** replacement is considered only after the other deficient axes are replaced and a **stimulation test** confirms the deficit. It is not started on a low IGF-1 alone. The insulin tolerance test cutoff used by the Endocrine Society is a peak at or below 5.1 micrograms per litre. That test is unsafe in ischaemic heart disease and in seizure disorder, so another stimulus is chosen when those risks are present.

steps.tx: **Traumatic brain** injury and subarachnoid haemorrhage can cause hypopituitarism at the time of injury or months later, so a normal early screen does not close the question. An empty sella is often an incidental imaging finding and does not by itself prove hormone deficiency. Test the axes when symptoms appear, and always secure cortisol before thyroid hormone. The order of loss in trauma is not the slow adenoma order.
